answer: Yes, early blight on young potato leaves can be mistaken for late blight because lesions may reach up to 1/2 inch in diameter [2]. However, early blight lesions are angular and become restricted by leaf veins, whereas late blight lesions are circular and surrounded by collapsed pale or chlorotic tissue [4]. Additionally, early blight lesions often display dark concentric rings alternating with light-tan bands, a feature not characteristic of late blight [2].

answer: The early blight fungus survives between growing seasons in infested plant debris, soil, and infected potato tubers [1]. It also persists in overwintering debris of susceptible solanaceous crops and weeds, including hairy nightshade [2]. The melanized spores and mycelia can withstand exposure to sunlight, drying, freezing, and thawing [3]. Use resistant varieties such as Allstar, Canoga, Cardinal, Delite, Earliglow, Honeoye, Jewell, Lester, Midway, or Redchief for June-bearing types [1]. For ever-bearing types, use Tribute or Tristar, which are tolerant to leaf scorch [1]. Ensure proper water management by avoiding water puddling for more than six hours; if overhead irrigation is used, irrigate in the morning so leaves can dry quickly [3]. Removing and burning all debris after harvest helps to reduce overwintering inoculum of leaf pathogens [2] and reduces the amount of disease-causing organisms available for the next season [4]. This publication deals broadly with the various aspects of disease management in corn production. Discussed are (1) the disease triangle, (2) considerations in assessing the need for disease control, (3) the range of potential control measures, and where they best apply, and (4) the major catego- ries of corn diseases and common control alternatives for each. THE DISEASE TRIANGLE The incidence and severity of a plant disease depends on the susceptibility of the plant variety (host), presence of a virulent disease-causing agent (pathogen), and a favorable air and soil environment. However, seldom has fungicide application to commercial dent corn fields shown economic returns, with exceptions being widespread southern corn leaf outbreaks in 1970 and 1971 [1]. Determining if chemical control is economically justified requires calculating anticipated returns without disease versus the dollar loss per acre from the disease, then comparing this to the total cost of control material and application per acre [5]. Crop Rotation Crop rotation is a sound cultural practice that also aids in the control of many diseases of corn (Nyvall, 1979). It is especially important for disease control when corn is grown in reduced tillage systems. A minimum of every other year in corn is neces- sary if crop rotation is to aid in disease control. Even then, rotation is not always effective because patho- gens (e.g., fungi causing leaf blights) can blow in from adjacent ﬁ elds. One popular cropping sequence where reduced tillage is practiced in the central and mid-southern U.S. is the production of three crops in 2 years (e.g., corn the ﬁ rst year then small grains and soybean double- cropped the second year). It is a sound cultural practice, especially important when corn is grown in reduced tillage systems [1]. A minimum rotation of every other year is necessary for disease control to be effective [1]. However, pathogens can blow in from adjacent fields even with rotation [1]. question: My plant has yellow leaves. What is it?

passages.text: On This Page Symptoms and Signs Comments on the Disease Management Important Links Symptoms and Signs Tomato yellow leaf curl is a disease of tomato caused by Tomato yellow leaf curl virus. In March 2007, it was identified for the first time in California and currently has a limited distribution. An educational brochure (PDF) was created at that time and is available to print. Infected tomato plants initially show stunted and erect or upright plant growth; plants infected at an early stage of growth will show severe stunting. However, the most diagnostic symptoms are those in leaves. Leaves of infected plants are small and curl upward; and show strong crumpling and interveinal and marginal yellowing . The internodes of infected plants become shortened and, together with the stunted growth, plants often take on a bushy appearance , which is sometimes referred to as 'bonsai' or broccoli'-like growth. Flowers formed on infected plants commonly do not develop and fall off (abscise). Fruit

or corrugated, and possibly cause the leaflets to curl downward at the edges. Younger leaves may have extensive yellow to white areas with dark green blisters. Cucumber mosaic virus (CMV) causes plants to become yellow, bushy and very stunted. Leaves may be extremely distorted and malformed. Leaflets are often very narrow – this is called “shoestring”. Often the leaves on one portion of the plant (e.g., the top or the bottom) show severe symptoms, while those higher or lower in the plant are less affected. Other leaf symptoms include a yellow and green mottling similar to tobacco mosaic symptoms. Severely affected plants produce few fruit. Identification of the Diseases. answer: Stems with sunken lesions may indicate early blight, where lesions are elliptical and can encircle stems causing distal tissue death [2]. They could also represent target spot, which causes small, watersoaked lesions that later become dark and crack, potentially leading to plant collapse [1]. answer:
If your potato plant has early blight, which is likely but not certain, the fungus (*Alternaria solani*) survives between growing seasons in several places:

- It survives in infested plant debris and soil, and in infected potato tubers [1][2].
- It also survives in overwintering debris of susceptible solanaceous crops and weeds, including hairy nightshade [1][2].
- It can survive on or just below the soil surface [3].
- Its overwintering spores and mycelia are darkly pigmented and can withstand sunlight and repeated drying, freezing and thawing [1][2].

Fields where potatoes had early blight the previous season are most prone to infection, because large amounts of overwintering inoculum are likely to be present [1][2].

Introduction Early blight occurs worldwide and is prevalent wherever potatoes are grown. Although the foliar phase of early blight was first reported in 1893, the tuber decay phase was not recognized until 1925. Foliar early blight and tuber decay are common in Colorado, Wyoming, and western Nebraska. Foliar early blight lesions decrease the leaf surface area, which reduces tuber yield potential. Although yield suppressions of 70 to 80 percent are reported, most losses rarely exceed 20 percent. Interaction of early blight with other diseases such as blackleg or Verticillium wilt can increase losses. Tuber infection and subsequent decay in storage can severely affect the quality of both fresh market and processing po- tatoes. Monitoring and control Effective management of early blight requires implementation of an integrated disease management approach. The "disease triangle" is the idea that a plant disease depends on three factors: a susceptible host (the plant variety), a virulent pathogen (the disease-causing agent), and a favorable air and soil environment [1]. All three must occur at the same time for disease to develop [1].

If any one of the three sides is missing, the disease fails to develop [2]. For example, planting a corn hybrid that is resistant to a given disease breaks the susceptible-host side of the triangle and prevents that disease [2].

The most common pathogen groups are fungi, bacteria, viruses, and nematodes [2]. Key environmental factors include air and soil temperature, rainfall, dew, relative humidity, soil type, soil pH, and soil fertility [2].

To reduce the risk of bacterial canker, treat tomato seed with chlorine [2].

- If the seed company hasn't already done so, dip the seed for 1 minute in a solution of 1 quart household bleach, 4 quarts water, and one-half teaspoon surfactant, with constant agitation [2].
- Use 1 gallon of solution per pound of seed, and mix a fresh solution for each batch [2].
- Wash the seed in running water for 5 minutes and dry it thoroughly [2]. Do the final rinse with acidified water (1 oz. vinegar per gallon of water) [2].
- Test the treatment on about 50 to 100 seeds first, because it may reduce germination [3].
- Don't use this treatment on pelleted seed, since it removes the coating [3].

Check the product labels and your local rules for using and disposing of the bleach and surfactant.

Generally, infected plants have a light or dark green mottling or mosaic with distortion of younger leaves, and stunting to varying degrees. Severely affected leaves may have a “fern- like” appearance and may show raised dark green areas. Fruit set may be severely reduced in affected plants. There may be internal browning of the fruit wall, yellow blotches and necrotic spots may occur on green or ripe fruit. Byther Biology Several viruses can cause mosaic symptoms in tomatoes, including tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), tomato mosaic virus (ToMV), and cucumber mosaic virus (CMV). Symptoms caused by TMV and ToMV are similar. Leaves show green mottling and may be curled, stunted, and slightly deformed. Plants may be stunted and are generally somewhat yellowed. Fruit is not usually affected but may be small and ripen unevenly. An internal browning of fruit may also occur. TMV and ToMV can be spread by tools, hands, and clothing. Symptoms of CMV include leaves with yellow mottling, bushy and stunted plants, and a reduced yield of small, slow-to-mature fruit.
